```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 100)
library(spax)
```

Floating catchment area (FCA) methods combine demand, facility supply and travel
weights into an accessibility index. This guide computes an enhanced two-step
FCA (E2SFCA) surface for general practice (GP) care in Cornwall, England, and
compares it with the original 2SFCA. All inputs ship with spax: no download,
routing server or private dataset is needed. For a fitted allocation model with
an outside option, see [Choosing a model](model-choice.html).

## The inputs and their units

```{r inputs}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")
gp <- sf::st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)

# Mainland only: the Isles of Scilly have no road link to the mainland.
gp <- gp[!gp$scilly, ]
travel <- travel[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice, then drop the
# empty margin the islands leave behind.
pop <- terra::trim(terra::mask(pop, sum(travel)))
travel <- terra::crop(travel, pop)
stopifnot(identical(names(travel), gp$practice),
  terra::compareGeom(pop, travel))
c(cells = sum(!is.na(terra::values(pop))), practices = nrow(gp),
  residents = round(terra::global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  gp_fte = round(sum(gp$gp_fte_extg), 1))
```

- **Demand** is the WorldPop 2020 population grid: estimated residents per
  cell of about 1 km (30 arc-seconds). It is a **count per cell**, not a
  density per square kilometre.
- **Supply** is `gp_fte_extg`: full-time equivalent GPs at each practice,
  excluding GPs in training (NHS England, June 2026).
- **Travel** is motorised travel time in whole minutes from each cell to each
  practice's main site, one layer per practice. Layer names are practice codes.

The population grid and the workforce data come from different sources and
dates, so the index below compares a 2026 workforce with a 2020 population
estimate. The analysis covers mainland Cornwall: 54 practices and the grid
cells that can reach them by road. [Preparing counts, facility IDs and
travel](spax-102-data-prep.html) explains these steps in detail.

## Calculate the E2SFCA surface

E2SFCA weights travel with a decay function. We use a Gaussian kernel with a
scale of 10 minutes: a practice 10 minutes away keeps `exp(-1/2)`, about 61%,
of its weight, and one 20 minutes away about 14%. The scale is our choice for
illustration, not a fitted value. `demand_normalize = "identity"` uses the
weights unchanged when practices gather demand, as in the original E2SFCA.

```{r e2sfca}
e2sfca <- spax_e2sfca(pop, gp, travel,
  decay_params = list(method = "gaussian", sigma = 10),
  demand_normalize = "identity", id_col = "practice",
  supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
e2sfca
```

The result is a `spax` object. Its `accessibility` member is a `SpatRaster` of
GP FTE per resident; `facilities` records the supply used and `parameters` the
decay and normalization choices. Per resident values are small, so we map GP
FTE per 1,000 residents.

```{r e2sfca-map}
practices <- sf::st_transform(cornwall_gp[!cornwall_gp$scilly, ], 4326)
per_1000 <- 1000 * e2sfca$accessibility
terra::plot(per_1000, axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  main = "E2SFCA: GP FTE per 1,000 residents (Gaussian, sigma = 10 min)")
terra::points(terra::vect(practices), pch = 3, cex = 0.5, col = "red")
```

Each cross is a practice. The index is highest in the west of the county,
from around Camborne and Redruth towards Truro and Falmouth, where several
practices with many GP FTE lie within a short drive. It is lowest on Bodmin Moor
and at the tips of the Land's End and Lizard peninsulas, where the nearest
practices are further away and the decay removes much of their weight.

```{r e2sfca-values}
a <- 1000 * terra::values(e2sfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
p <- terra::values(pop, mat = FALSE)
round(quantile(a, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE), 2)
c(resident_weighted_mean = weighted.mean(a, p, na.rm = TRUE),
  total_fte_per_1000 = 1000 * sum(gp$gp_fte_extg) / sum(p, na.rm = TRUE))
```

The quantiles describe grid cells, and most cells are rural. Weighting by
residents answers a different question: the index the average resident sees.
Here that average equals total GP FTE per 1,000 residents, because both steps
use the same weights and every practice has residents within reach. The index
redistributes the supply; it does not create or lose any.

The index has supply-per-demand units. It is not a share of people who use a
practice, a waiting time or an observed rate of care.

## Compare with the original 2SFCA

The original 2SFCA replaces the decay with a fixed catchment: a practice counts
fully within 15 minutes and not at all beyond. Both maps below show GP FTE per
1,000 residents on one colour scale.

```{r twosfca, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 3.6}
twosfca <- spax_2sfca(pop, gp, travel, threshold = 15,
  id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
both <- c(per_1000, 1000 * twosfca$accessibility)
names(both) <- c("E2SFCA, Gaussian 10 min", "2SFCA, 15 min")
terra::plot(both, axes = FALSE, col = hcl.colors(50, "viridis"),
  range = range(terra::values(both), na.rm = TRUE), mar = c(1, 1, 2, 5))
```

```{r twosfca-values}
b <- 1000 * terra::values(twosfca$accessibility, mat = FALSE)
round(rbind(E2SFCA = quantile(a, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE),
  `2SFCA` = quantile(b, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95), na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
c(residents_beyond_15_min = round(sum(p[b == 0], na.rm = TRUE)),
  correlation = round(cor(a, b, use = "complete.obs"), 2))
```

The two surfaces broadly agree (correlation 0.79 across cells), but 2SFCA
shows sharp steps at the 15-minute edges and a wider spread, and the few
residents with no practice within 15 minutes get an index of zero. The decay
version changes gradually instead. Both depend on choices, the threshold or the
decay scale, that this guide does not estimate from data.
